BMC Public Health
Correlations between frailty index 
and inflammatory markers derived from blood 
cell count in the United States
Shaojie Han1,2†, Zenghui Zhang1,2†, Siyuan Cheng1,2, Yuchen Han1,2, Qianyun Wang1,2, Yangbo Xi1,2, 
Panpan Li1,2, Fengjuan Li1,2* and Jun Guo1,2* 
Abstract 
Background  Complete blood cell count (CBC)-derived inflammatory biomarkers are crucial indicators of adverse 
outcomes and possess predictive value for a wide range of diseases. The objective of this study was to evaluate 
the links between CBC-derived inflammatory biomarkers and frailty index.
Methods  Information was gathered from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) span-
ning the years 1999 to 2016. The research investigated the correlation between inflammatory biomarkers derived 
from CBC, including the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), monocyte-to-lymphocyte ratio (MLR), systemic inflam-
matory response index (SIRI), and systemic immune-inflammation index (SII), and Rockwood’s frailty index, using 
logistic regression analyses.
Results  In total, the cross-sectional study involved 13,507 U.S. adults aged 50 and older, with 3,729 individuals (24%) 
meeting the criteria for frailty. After adjusting for confounding factors, elevated levels of logNLR (odds ratio [OR] 
3.45, 95% confidence interval [CI] 2.52–4.73), logMLR (OR 3.58, 95% CI 2.44–5.25), logSIRI (OR 2.77, 95% CI 2.17–3.55), 
and logSII (OR 1.89, 95% CI 1.44–2.48) were significantly associated with an increased frailty index in the entire study 
population. We also found that frailty index and inflammatory biomarkers derived from CBC have a non-linear rela-
tionship by restricted cubic spline.
Conclusions  Our findings indicate a correlation between frailty index and NLR, MLR, SIRI, and SII among elderly 
adults. Considering their wide accessibility in both clinical and laboratory practice, these biomarkers may be recom-
mended as potential indicators for the development of frailty.
Keywords  Inflammation biomarkers, Epidemiology, Frailty index, NHANES
Background
Frailty is marked by a deterioration in performance 
across various physiological systems, coupled with an 
elevated susceptibility to external stressors [1, 2]. It is 
linked with heightened rates of mortality, hospitaliza-
tion, incidents of falls, and placement in long-term 
care facilities [1, 2]. Individuals with frailty also experi-
ence a significant personal burden, which encompasses 
a diminished quality of life and feelings of isolation [3].

older individuals residing in the community, participat-
ing in studies conducted in high-income countries, the 
weighted average estimation for frailty was determined to 
be 11% [4]. The frailty is projected to surge in conjunction 
with the rapid growth of the elderly population. Frailty 
represents an emerging worldwide health challenge, with 
significant ramifications for both clinical healthcare and 
public health [5]. Comprehending the pathophysiological 
underpinnings of frailty is crucial for the formulation of 
prevention and intervention strategies. Numerous stud-
ies have provided evidence that chronic systemic inflam-
mation serves as the fundamental cause of frailty [6–8]. 
Soysal et  al. discovered that frailty and pre-frailty were 
linked to increased serum levels of IL-6 in comparison to 
robust individuals, and they were likewise notably linked 
with increased levels of white blood cells and fibrinogen 
[9].
Recently, in a variety of medical conditions, prognos-
tic indicators derived from a complete blood cell count 
(CBC), such as the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio 
(NLR), monocyte-to-lymphocyte ratio (MLR), systemic 
immune inflammation index (SII), and systemic inflam-
matory response index (SIRI), have been utilized. [10–
12]. These biomarkers are formulated by combining two 
or three parameters related to lymphocytes, monocytes, 
platelets, and neutrophils. The NLR, SII, and SIRI exhibit 
predictive capabilities for severe COVID-19 and the 
need for invasive mechanical ventilation support among 
hospitalized Mexican COVID-19 patients [13]. Findings 
from observational studies have indicated a substantial 
link between these circulatory inflammatory biomarkers 
and heightened risks of cardiovascular disease, demen-
tia, and mortality in the elderly population [14–16]. A 
cross-sectional study, including 345 coronary heart dis-
ease patients aged ≥ 60, revealed an association between 
frailty phenotype, as defined by Fried’s criteria, and NLR 
in these elderly patients [17]. And another study revealed 
that elevated NLR levels were correlated with frailty in 
older adults residing in the community based on Rock-
wood’s frailty index [18]. Zhang and colleagues addition-
ally observed that individuals with elevated NLR and SII 
levels faced an increased odds of having frailty phenotype 
over the course of the longitudinal study based on Fried’s 
criteria [19].
However, previous studies focused primarily on NLR, 
with no research yet evaluating the relationship between 
SIRI and frailty index. Compared to NLR, SIRI reflects 
both acute and chronic inflammation. Additionally, prior 
studies were limited to small Chinese samples, leaving 
uncertainty about their relevance to Americans. While 
the more common use of Fried’s phenotype addresses 
the biological cycle of frailty, our study adopts Rock-
wood’s multidimensional approach to better capture the 
accumulation of deficits with aging. We used data from 
the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 
(NHANES) to investigate the relationship between CBC-
derived inflammatory biomarkers (NLR, MLR, SIRI, and 
SII) and frailty index in U.S. adults aged 50 and older.
Materials and Methodology
Study population
Our evaluations relied on cross-sectional data gathered 
from NHANES, covering the period from 1999 to 2016. 
NHANES represents a health survey administered by 
the National Center for Health Statistics, which oper-
ates as a division within the Centers for Disease Control 
and Prevention [20]. We used NHANES data collected 
over multiple two-year cycles, and biomarker measure-
ments, baseline data, and frailty assessments were typi-
cally gathered in the year participants entered the survey. 
For example, a participant enrolled in 2001 would have 
all relevant data collected during that year. The primary 
goal is to assess the health and nutritional status of the 
non-institutionalized civilian population in the United 
States, providing a comprehensive overview that is rep-
resentative of the entire country. NHANES obtained 
ethical approval from the National Center for Health Sta-
tistics, and all participants in the study provided written 
informed consent. This study conforms to the Declara-
tion of Helsinki.
Assessment of CBC‑derived inflammatory biomarkers
Automated hematology analyzers are employed to meas-
ure the complete blood count, quantifying the quan-
tity of various blood cell types (including red blood 
cells, white blood cells, and platelets) within a speci-
fied blood volume. We computed the SIRI, SII, NLR, 
and MLR using the following formulas: SIRI = (neutro-
phil counts × monocyte counts)/lymphocyte counts, 
SII = (platelet counts × neutrophil counts)/lymphocyte 
counts, NLR = neutrophil counts/lymphocyte counts, 
and MLR = monocyte counts/lymphocyte counts [12].
Frailty assessment
We used a modified frailty index based on the Rockwood 
frailty index, excluding ten items from the original 46 that 
were related to intake or nutritional status (as shown in 
Supplemental Table S1). This index has been validated in 
the NHANES cohort and applied in many previous stud-
ies [21–23]. If the patient meets a criterion, it is scored as 
1 point, if not, it is scored as 0 points, and the points are 
added together. In our study, we used frailty index equal 
to 0.3 as the cutoff point to divide the study population 
into two groups, the fit group (frailty index ≤ 0.3)and the 
frail group (frailty index > 0.3).

Covariate assessment
Baseline data about the participants were obtained 
via questionnaires and laboratory assessment. Body 
mass index (BMI) was categorized into three groups: 
healthy weight (BMI ≤ 25.0 kg/m2), overweight (25.0 kg/
m2 ≤ BMI < 30.0  kg/m2), and obese (BMI ≥ 30.0  kg/m2). 
The race variable was segmented into five subgroups, 
including non-Hispanic White, Mexican American, other 
Hispanic, non-Hispanic Black, and other racial back-
grounds. Smoking status was dichotomized into two 
groups: nonsmokers were individuals who had never 
consumed a minimum of 100 cigarettes in their lifetime, 
while smokers were those who had smoked at least 100 
cigarettes. Drinking status was categorized into two 
groups: non-drinkers were characterized as individu-
als who had not consumed a minimum of 12 alcoholic 
beverages in the past year or throughout their lifetime, 
while drinkers were those who had imbibed at least 12 
drinks in the past year. Physical exercise was categorized 
into three groups: "low," "moderate," and "active." Other 
covariates include age, sex, family poverty income ratio 
(PIR), and educational level (divided into less than high 
school, high school graduate, college or higher). The total 
energy intake was determined by computing the mean 
of two days. Data concerning hypertension and diabetes 
were obtained through self-reported questionnaires.
Statistical analysis
The medians of continuous variables (interquartile range 
[IQR]) are displayed. The numerical values (percent-
ages) for categorical variables are displayed. The Mann–
Whitney U test (non-normal distribution) or the t-test 
(normal distribution) will be used to compare continu-
ous variables. The chi-square test was utilized to com-
pare categorical variables. Based on the quartiles (Q), 
we also separated the NLR, MLR, SIRI, and SII into four 
groups. Q1: 1.53, Q2: > 1.53, ≤ 2.08, Q3: > 2.08, ≤ 2.83 and 
Q4: > 2.83 for NLR (Supplemental Table  S2). According 
to Supplemental Table  S3, Q1: ≤ 0.22; Q2: > 0.22, ≤ 0.29; 
Q3: > 0.29, ≤ 0.38; and Q4: > 0.38 for MLR. According to 
Supplemental Table S4, SIRI: Q1: < 0.76; Q2: > 0.76, ≤ 1.13; 
Q3: > 0.76, ≤ 1.68; Q4: > 1.68. According to Supplemental 
Table S5, for SII, Q1 is < 339.58, Q2 is > 339.58, ≤ 481.85, 
Q3 is > 481.85 ≤ 689.61, and Q4 is > 689.61. The research 
population’s various features between the NLR, MLR, 
SIRI, and SII quartiles were then discussed. The adjusted 
odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) of the 
relationship between CBC-derived inflammatory bio-
markers and frailty index were determined using a mul-
tiple logistic regression model. In the restricted cubic 
spline regression analysis, we tested the non-linear rela-
tionship by comparing a linear model with a model that 
included non-linear (spline) terms. A p-value was cal-
culated to assess non-linear relationship and a p-value 
less than 0.05 indicated that the non-linear relationship 
was statistically significant. Due to their nonnormal dis-
tribution, the NLR, SIRI, SII, and MLR, were log-trans-
formed before being used in the analyses. All analyses 
were conducted in two models. Model 1: adjusted for age, 
sex, NHANES cycle, and race. Model 2: redesigned to 
account for Model 1 and include variables such as edu-
cation level, family poverty income ratio, BMI, physical 
activity, total energy intake, smoking or drinking status, 
diabetes, and hypertension. To understand how different 
factors might affect the results, we carried out sensitiv-
ity analysis. To explore how various factors might influ-
ence the results, we conducted sensitivity analysis using 
logistic and restricted cubic spline regression, adjusting 
for angina/angina pectoris, heart attack, coronary heart 
disease, stroke, thyroid condition, cancer, arthritis, weak/
failing kidneys, pulse rate, pulse pressure, platelet count, 
blood urea nitrogen, bicarbonate, red cell distribution 
width, lactate dehydrogenase, and uric acid. Statistical 
significance was defined as p value of two-tailed < 0.05. 
Each analysis was completed with R (version 4.3).
Results
Characteristics of study participants
During the period spanning 1999 to 2016, 92,062 people 
were involved in the NHANES. A total of 70,392 par-
ticipants were omitted because they were younger than 
50 years old. Subsequently, a total of 2,508 participants 
did not possess adequate information regarding their 
complete blood cell data. In addition, among the remain-
ing participants, 5503 individuals had insufficient data for 
frailty assessment, and 152 people had missing covariate 
information. Finally, 13,507 patients were included in the 
analysis (Fig. 1).
The baseline features of person with inflammatory bio-
markers determined from CBC are displayed in Table 1. 
The study cohort had a median age of 66 years [IQR 61, 
74] with a maximum age of 85 years, was 46% male, and 
predominantly consisted of non-Hispanic white individu-
als (79%). The medians of NLR, MLR, SIRI and SII were 
2.08 [IQR 1.53, 2.83], 0.29 [IQR 0.22, 0.38], 1.13[IQR 
0.76, 1.68], and 481.85 [IQR 339.58, 689.61], respectively. 
In comparison to fit (FI ≤ 0.3) group, those who were frail 
were more likely to be elderly females, have lower levels 
of education, be current smokers, abstain from alcohol, 
exhibit physical inactivity, possess a higher BMI, and have 
diabetes and hypertension (p < 0.05). In frail patients, the 
counts of white blood cells, neutrophils, monocytes, and 
lymphocytes were notably higher (P < 0.05). Participants 
with and without frailty differed significantly in NLR, 
MLR, SIRI, and SII.

CBC‑derived inflammatory biomarkers and frailty index
Table  2 presents the correlation between the NLR, 
MLR, SIRI, and SII and frailty index. After control-
ling for covariates, a significant correlation was seen 
between frailty index and logNLR (OR 3.45, 95% CI 
2.52–4.73), logMLR (OR 3.58, 95% CI 2.44–5.25), log-
SIRI (OR 2.77, 95% CI 2.17–3.55), and logSII (OR 1.89, 
95% CI 1.44–2.48) in all people. All inflammatory indi-
cators derived from CBC were categorized into four 
groups and analyzed for their connection with frailty 
index. Positive relationships between the increase in 
frailty index and CBC-derived markers (NLR, MLR, 
SIRI, and SII) were found by using model 1. Our con-
clusion is further demonstrated in model 2. As shown 
in Table  3, the OR and 95% CI for the highest quar-
tile compared to the lowest quartile after adjusting 
for potential confounding variables were NLR (OR 
1.73 95%CI 1.45–2.06, P trend < 0.001), MLR (OR 1.61 
95%CI 1.36–1.91, P trend < 0.001), SIRI (OR1.72 95%CI 
1.43–2.06, P trend < 0.001), and SII (OR 1.31 95%CI 
1.09–1.57, P trend < 0.001), (Table  3). We observed a 
nonlinear correlation between frailty index and mark-
ers of inflammation from CBC by restricted cubic 
spline (Fig. 2).
In the sensitivity analysis, in addition to the variables 
in model 2, we further adjusted for as many variables as 
possible. We found that NLR (OR 1.89, 95% CI 1.37–
2.60), RISI (OR 1.44, 95% CI 1.11–1.88), and SII (OR 1.63, 
95% CI 1.18–2.23) still showed statistically significant 
differences, as shown in Supplemental Table S6. In sen-
sitivity analysis, the OR and 95% CI for the highest quar-
tile compared to the lowest quartile were NLR (OR 1.28 
95%CI 1.05–1.57, P trend < 0.001), MLR (OR 1.00 95%CI 
0.84 -1.19, P trend = 0.320), SIRI (OR 1.21 95%CI 1.03–
2.06, P trend < 0.001), and SII (OR 1.19 95%CI 1.00–1.46, 
P trend < 0.001), (Supplemental Table S7). We also iden-
tified a nonlinear correlation between the frailty index 
and inflammatory markers from CBC in the sensitiv-
ity analysis using restricted cubic splines (Supplemental 
Figure S1).

Discussion
Principal findings
We carried out a cross-sectional investigation involv-
ing 13,507 adults aged over 50 to explore the relation-
ship between frailty index and inflammatory biomarkers 
derived from CBC in the United States. Our primary 
discoveries revealed a strong correlation between ele-
vated NLR, SII, MLR, and SIRI and an augmented odd 
of having frailty based on Rockwood’s frailty index. Fur-
thermore, given the widespread availability and ease of 
measurement of NLR, SIRI, SII, and MLR, they may be 
proposed as potential indicators for an increase in the 
frailty index.
Currently available research
Until now, numerous investigations have explored the 
connection between frailty index and inflammatory bio-
markers derived from CBC [17–19, 24, 25]. Zhang et al. 
discovered a significant association between elevated 
logNLR (OR 2.92, p < 0.001), logPLR (OR 2.54, p < 0.001), 
and logSII (OR 2.34, p < 0.001) and an increased odd of 
frailty in all participants after adjusting for covariates 
based on the Fried phenotype [19]. Furthermore, prior 
investigations have established associations between 
inflammatory markers in blood cells and frailty index 
within specific populations. Guan et al. reported that in

conducted a research to assess the relationship between 
NLR and frailty index in a cohort of 345 elderly individu-
als with coronary heart disease based on the Fried phe-
notype [17]. Patients in the fourth quartile of NLR and 
RDW exhibited fully-adjusted OR for the development of 
frailty of 2.89 (p = 0.011) and 2.49 (p = 0.040) [17].
Xu et al. observed that an elevated NLR was linked to 
greater odds of both prevalent and incident frailty in a 
longitudinal cohort study comprising over 1800 older 
adults residing in the community based on Rockwood’s 
frailty index [18]. Nishijima and their team conducted a 
cross-sectional study to explore the relationship between 
NLR and frailty, based on Rockwood’s frailty index, in 
older cancer patients [24]. They found that those in the 
highest tertile NLR group had almost four times higher 
chances of being frail in elderly cancer patients [24]. In 
short, they indicated a possible association between 
CBC-derived inflammatory indicators and frailty index. 
However, the small sample size and disease-specific 
research populations in the aforementioned studies 
hampered the generalizability of the study findings. In 
the above studies, with the exception of Nishijima et al., 
the participants in the other investigations were of Chi-
nese ethnicity, which restricts the generalizability of the 
findings. Moreover, the aforementioned studies did not 
investigate the relationship between SIRI and frailty. 
Most of these studies used Fried’s criteria to assess frailty, 
with only two studies utilizing Rockwood’s frailty index 
[18, 24]. Our study complements the above studies by 
including a cross-sectional study from a national popu-
lation in the United States based on Rockwood’s frailty 
index. Our study is the first to report a close association 
between SIRI and frailty, in addition to exploring tradi-
tional markers such as NLR, MLR, and SII. In addition, 
our study found a nonlinear relationship between inflam-
matory markers derived from CBC and frailty index 
through restricted cubic spline.
In addition to frailty, there is a substantial body of evi-
dence investigating the link between inflammatory bio-
markers derived from CBC and sarcopenia, a prevalent 
geriatric syndrome closely associated with frailty [19, 27, 
28]. To investigate these correlations, Zhao et  al. per-
formed cross-sectional research with 4,224 people in 
China. They discovered that increased NLR, PLR and SII 
were all associated with a heightened risk of developing 
sarcopenia [28]. Figure 3 demonstrates that the relation-
ship between inflammatory markers and frailty index is 
more pronounced in specific subgroups, including older 
participants and females. This suggests that these groups 
may be more vulnerable to the effects of systemic inflam-
mation, contributing to their increased frailty index. As 
individuals age, the body’s immune system may gradually

weaken, leading to enhanced inflammatory responses 
[2]. Older adults may exhibit greater vulnerability when 
dealing with chronic inflammation, which can affect their 
physical function and quality of life [29]. In women, ele-
vated inflammatory markers were associated with frailty 
index [30]. Women may be more sensitive to inflamma-
tory responses in certain physiological and psychological 
aspects [30]. After identifying high-risk groups (such as 
older adults and women), clinicians can take preventive 
measures, such as improving diet and managing inflam-
mation, to reduce the risk of developing frailty.
The possible mechanisms
It has been suggested that NLR, SII, MLR, and SIRI 
are indicators of inflammation. The exact mechanisms 
underlying the relationship between CBC-derived 
inflammatory biomarkers (NLR, MLR, SIRI, and SII) 
and frailty index remain largely unclear. There is a 
broad consensus that chronic low-grade inflammation 
may play a pivotal role in the advancement of frailty 
[8]. One such possible pathophysiological alteration 
that may be intimately associated with frailty index is 
inflammation [31]. Research has indicated that elevated 
inflammatory marker levels in the bloodstream are cor-
related with increased muscle mass and strength loss, 
reduced physical activity, accelerated declines in mobil-
ity, and higher rates of depression among older individ-
uals [32, 33], all of which are fundamental components 
used in the literature to define frailty index according 
to prevailing criteria [34]. Many theories have been 
proposed to clarify how inflammation, sarcopenia, and 
frailty are related [8]. Prior studies have demonstrated a 
link between inflammation and reduced synthesis and 
function of insulin-like growth factor I (IGF1) which is 
pivotal in muscle regeneration and the preservation of 
muscle integrity [35]. Furthermore, there is evidence 
indicating that IL-1α and IL-6 can inhibit IGF1-medi-
ated anabolism, while TNF inhibitors have the potential 
to reduce the production of both IGF1 and IGF-binding 
protein in vitro [36]. Inflammation hinders endothelial 
reactivity and muscle perfusion, disrupting the absorp-
tion of long branched-chain amino acids crucial for 
muscle energy and protein synthesis [8, 37]. Addition-
ally, researches have indicated a substantial correlation 
between NLR and IL-6, CRP, and TNF-α [18, 38]. NLR, 
PLR, and SII are indicative of the equilibrium between 
the innate and adaptive immune systems [39, 40]. Age-
related alterations in the immune system may contrib-
ute to heightened levels of low-grade, chronic systemic 
inflammation [19].
In this study, we also recognize various constraints. 
First, the cross-sectional design of this study introduces 
limitations, so the interpretation of the results should 
be approached with caution. Future longitudinal pro-
spective studies are needed to more thoroughly con-
firm our findings. Second, the NHANES results relied 
on participants self-reports, potentially introducing 
recall bias. Third, blood cells were measured only once 
in the samples we included, and it may be necessary 
to repeat the measurements multiple times to more 
accurately reflect changes in inflammatory biomarkers. 
Fourthly, our study was limited to utilizing the frailty 
index to define the frailty status. It is advisable that 
future investigations employ the Fried frailty phenotype 
to better explore the connection between inflammatory 
biomarkers and frailty. Fifth, we categorize drinking 
status based on less or more than 12 drinks in the past 
year, which seems too crude and may lead to bias in the 
results when adjusting for covariates. Finally, NHANES 
serves as a nationally representative survey, but the 
applicability of these findings to other countries may be 
constrained. Consequently, additional research is war-
ranted to elucidate the exact relationship among these 
variables.
Conclusion
In summary, we discovered that elevated NLR, MLR, 
SIRI, and SII levels were linked to a higher frailty index 
in elderly individuals in this nationwide research. These 
results add to the evidence regarding the possible 
effectiveness of these biomarkers in forecasting frailty. 
Furthermore, given that NLR, MLR, SII, and SIRI are 
widely employed in practice and are easily obtain-
able through laboratory assessments, they could be 
suggested as cost-efficient prognosticators for frailty 
incidents.
